item.title: Databricks Introduces LiveRamp Embedded Identity via Packaged Clean Rooms
item.description:
Databricks Introduces LiveRamp Embedded Identity via Packaged Clean Rooms

🔍 Overview

Traditionally, Databricks customers resolving customer records to a person-based ID like RampID had to manually export PII, wait for a match file, and reload it—adding pipeline complexity, data copies, and delays. LiveRamp Embedded Identity on Databricks now eliminates this workflow by integrating identity resolution directly into the data environment.

🧩 How it works

Traditional Workflow (Before)

  • Data teams exported PII to an external service.
  • Waited for a match file from the service.
  • Reloaded the resolved data back into their environment.
  • Each step required maintaining pipelines, managing copies of sensitive data, and introducing delays.

New Workflow (LiveRamp Embedded Identity)

  • LiveRamp Embedded Identity brings identity resolution to the customer’s Databricks environment.
  • Customers retain full control over their data, with no need to export PII externally.
  • Minimal setup allows customers to receive resolved RampIDs directly in their Unity Catalog.
  • These RampIDs serve as match keys for downstream use cases, such as customer 360, audience building, and activation.

Packaged Clean Rooms

  • A Databricks clean room is a secure, isolated environment where multiple parties collaborate without sharing raw data or intellectual property (IP).

  • In a standard clean room:

    • Collaborators are peers.
    • Each party approves the other’s code before execution.
    • Data remains private, but collaborators see table aliases and schema details.

  • A packaged clean room extends privacy to the entire analysis by separating the identity provider (LiveRamp) from the customer.

    • No approval steps are required.
    • Neither party sees the other’s data, tables, or schemas.
    • The provider ships a pre-built analysis as a product, and the customer runs it against their data.
    • This setup enables scalable deployments across multiple customers with minimal setup.

Identity Resolution via Packaged Clean Rooms

  • Central Clean Room: A Databricks-managed environment where LiveRamp’s identity logic and customer data interact.
  • OpenSharing Protocol: Both parties add Unity Catalog assets (tables, models, libraries) to the clean room, granting read-only access without replication.
  • Live Data Access: OpenSharing ensures the clean room reads the current version of the customer’s input table, not an older extract.
  • Governance & Audit: Unity Catalog governance is maintained on both sides, and activity is audited in system tables.

Execution Flow

  • A single run writes to two schemas:
    • One schema delivers resolved RampIDs to the customer’s environment.
    • The other schema delivers the identity resolution logic to LiveRamp.
    • Both outputs are shared via OpenSharing and can be queried immediately.
    • For long-term use beyond 30 days, results must be copied to the customer’s cloud storage.
  • Both parties track run status, timing, and notebook execution history.
  • Shared troubleshooting occurs via run status and output schema, without exposing data.

⚙️ Key details

Components

Component Role Access Control
Central Clean Room Hosts the identity resolution logic and data interaction. Databricks-managed; no administrative access from either party.
OpenSharing Protocol Enables live, read-only access to customer and LiveRamp assets without replication. Unity Catalog governance enforced on both sides.
Unity Catalog Governs data assets shared between parties. Customer controls which tables to add; provider controls exposed assets.

Benefits

  • No Data Export: Customer data and resolved results remain private within Unity Catalog.
  • No PII Copies: Eliminates the need for managing sensitive data copies.
  • No Delays: Immediate access to resolved RampIDs for analytics and AI workloads.
  • Scalability: Single packaged clean room can serve multiple customers with identical setups.
  • Privacy: Both parties retain full control over their data and code, with no shared visibility.
  • Auditability: Comprehensive logs track run status, timing, and notebook execution.

🚀 Availability

LiveRamp Embedded Identity via Packaged Clean Rooms is available on Databricks, enabling customers to perform identity resolution with minimal setup. For detailed setup steps, refer to:

  • LiveRamp’s guide: Perform RampID identity resolution in Databricks
  • Databricks Packaged Clean Rooms documentation

💡 Why it matters

This innovation transforms identity resolution from a manual, pipeline-heavy process into a streamlined, governed workflow. By leveraging packaged clean rooms, customers can:

  • Accelerate analytics: Access resolved RampIDs directly in their Unity Catalog.
  • Enhance collaboration: Securely share insights with partners without exposing raw data.
  • Simplify governance: Maintain Unity Catalog controls while eliminating external data transfers.
  • Reduce operational overhead: Avoid managing match files, PII copies, and approval workflows.

The result is a more efficient, private, and scalable approach to identity resolution for AI and analytics workloads.

#databricks #identity-resolution #clean-rooms #ai-data-privacy #unity-catalog

Source: How packaged clean rooms bring RampID to your lakehouse

item.title: Meta's Muse AI Assistant Raises Privacy Concerns Over Data Harvesting
item.description:
Meta’s Muse AI Assistant Raises Privacy Concerns Over Data Harvesting

Meta’s recently released AI personal assistant, Muse, has sparked debate regarding the collection of user and third-party data. Since its release last month, the agent has reached No. 1 on Apple’s App Store with millions of downloads, utilizing a virtual avatar to request access to sensitive information including bank accounts, passwords, contact lists, and chat logs.

🧩 How it works

Muse is designed as an autonomous helper intended to perform menial tasks such as filling out invoices and sending emails. To function, the agent ingests large amounts of personal context, which Meta states is gathered from public information and data the user chooses to share. Security researchers have discovered that the agent maintains an internal process that updates profiles of every person in a user’s life on an hourly basis.

⚙️ Key details

  • Data Scope: The agent accesses emails, messages, contacts, and photos, often including information belonging to the user’s friends and family.
  • User Interface: Critics suggest the interface uses dark patterns to encourage users to share more data than they may realize.
  • Permissions: Meta maintains that data access is opt-in. For example, the company stated that full disk access on a Mac is required for the agent to access text messages.
  • Incidents: Users have reported issues such as the exposure of a tech reviewer’s home address and the potential for the agent to access text messages, which Meta attributes to misconfigured app permissions.

💡 Why it matters

Experts from the Signal Foundation and the Electronic Frontier Foundation have raised concerns that these AI agents extend mass surveillance to sensitive data. Because the agent processes information about the user’s contacts, individuals who did not consent to using the service may still have their personal data ingested. There is currently no meaningful way for those individuals to opt out of this data collection process.

#Meta #Muse #Privacy #AIAgents #DataSecurity

Source: Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents

item.title: OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse
item.description:
OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman introduced Dots, a new AI agent designed to set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI. The announcement included direct critiques of Meta’s Muse, with OpenAI positioning its new assistant as a more secure and trustworthy alternative to its primary competitor.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI executives used the launch of Dots to highlight security concerns surrounding Meta’s Muse, which had previously launched as a safer alternative to the agent OpenClaw. While Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised Muse was built for privacy and security, the platform has faced scrutiny over data collection and vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s leadership, including Codex product lead Alexander Embiricos, stated the company is focused on providing the most secure assistant while avoiding the mistakes of rivals.

⚙️ Key details

AI Agent Developer Stated Privacy and Security Approach
Dots OpenAI Zero data retention policy options for enterprises and individual user-set rules.
Muse Meta User data stored in isolated Linux VMs with browser, CPU, memory, and storage.
OpenClaw (Not specified) Predecessor to Muse; described as less safe than subsequent alternatives.

🧩 Capabilities and Controls

OpenAI and Meta have implemented different strategies to manage user data and agent behavior:

  • OpenAI Dots: Users can exert individual control over the agent, such as setting rules to prevent it from making purchases over a specific dollar amount. Enterprise customers can access frameworks with stronger data controls and options to ensure no data is stored on OpenAI servers.
  • Meta Muse: The agent defaults to allowing Meta to train models on user input, though an opt-out is available. While the company plans to introduce cryptographic methods to prevent internal access to VM data, Meta currently retains access.

🚀 Availability

OpenAI has launched Dots with a focus on its high-end user base, currently making it available only on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers. In contrast, Meta’s Muse saw rapid adoption following its release, gaining 600,000 daily active users in the United States within weeks and topping App Store charts.

💡 Why it matters

The push for more private AI agents comes as labs try to convince users to share increasingly personal information. Despite Meta’s privacy promises for Muse, security researchers exposed a zero-day vulnerability, and reports indicated the agent created detailed profiles of users’ social networks and shared private data, such as physical addresses and private messages, as part of its intended functions. OpenAI’s strategy with Dots relies on one-upping these rivals by promising stricter data boundaries, though some users still report discomfort when asked to provide sensitive financial information to these agents.

#OpenAI #Dots #Meta #AIAgents #DataPrivacy

Source: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

item.title: Apple to Tighten Mac Full Disk Access Controls Amid AI Agent Risks
item.description:
Apple to Tighten Mac Full Disk Access Controls Amid AI Agent Risks

Apple has announced plans to tighten the way apps are granted Full Disk Access on macOS, citing growing risks as AI agents become more capable and autonomous. The company warned that this broad permission can expose highly sensitive data and bypasses the privacy controls normally used to protect user data.

🔍 Overview

Full Disk Access is one of the broadest permissions available in macOS. While it is intended for software like backup tools, it allows apps to reach data that is otherwise protected behind separate privacy controls. Apple reports that some developers are currently using this permission in ways that could put users at risk by exposing several types of data:

  • Personal files
  • Email messages
  • Messages
  • Browsing history
  • Sensitive data across large parts of a system

⚙️ Key Details

Apple directly linked the upcoming changes to the rise of agentic AI software. Unlike traditional apps that might need access for a single function, AI agents can carry out tasks across multiple apps, files, and services.

Feature Description
Permission Level One of the broadest in macOS; bypasses standard privacy controls.
Original Intent Designed for utilities such as backup software.
Current Concern AI agents may expose significantly more personal info than traditional apps.
Privacy Stance Positioned as a central part of Apple’s on-device and cloud-based AI processing.

🧩 How it Works

The company intends to introduce additional controls that require more explicit user action before an app can receive Full Disk Access. The goal of these protections is to ensure users clearly understand the risks involved and make a deliberate, informed decision before granting such broad access to their data.

🚀 Availability

Apple has not announced exactly what the new Full Disk Access controls will look like or when they will arrive. The company stated only that the additional protections will be introduced going forward as it continues to expand artificial intelligence across the Mac through Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.

#Apple #macOS #AIAgents #Privacy #Cybersecurity

Source: Apple plans tougher Mac Full Disk Access controls as AI agents expand
